title: Sinuous growth lines on non-cylindrical horns result from torsional strain

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Sinuous growth lines on non-cylindrical horns result from torsional strain

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Horns that grow as curves of double curvature undergo torsional strain, because the sheath is attached to the core, and this strain warps the rings into the sinuous growth lines predicted by St Venant for a twisted non-circular prism; such lines are absent from cylindrical ox horns.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But there is yet another and a very remarkable phenomenon which we may discern in the growth of a horn, when it takes the form of a curve of double curvature, namely, an effect of torsional strain; and this it is which gives rise to the sinuous “lines of growth,” or sinuous boundaries of the separate horny rings, of which we have already spoken.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XIII, “The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion”; topic “Torsion and growth lines of horns”. Scope: horns of sheep, Ovis ammon, antelopes; contrasted with oxen

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch13-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.50

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing scans can test the predicted geometric association and elastic shape for selected specimens. Establishing torsional strain as the cause requires mechanical variables generally missing from public data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Quantify centerline torsion, cross-sectional eccentricity and growth-line sinuosity from high-resolution horn surfaces, and compare the observed warping with elastic-prism predictions. Covariation and correct predicted line orientation support the mechanism; sinuous rings without torsion or absent rings under high torsion refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Surface resolution may be insufficient for growth rings.

Attachment forces and material properties are not recorded.

Weathering can mimic or erase sinuous lines.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The predicted pattern is specific: sinuous boundaries on twisted non-circular horns, and their absence on cylindrical cattle horns. Photographs in museum portals show those rings for some species, but they have not been measured into an open table, and scans often stop at the bone. A scored sample could test the association, with remaining ambiguity between torsion and other causes of wavy increments.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Score growth-ring waviness, cross-sectional ellipticity, and helical curvature on sheep, argali, antelope, and ox horns. The torsion account is supported if sinuous rings occur on non-circular, helically curved horns and are absent on cylindrical ox horns; sinuous rings on round horns, or smooth rings on strongly twisted elliptical horns, would refute the predicted association.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Growth rings are a surface feature often missing from skeletal CT, and they are not a database field.

Seasonal growth and wear can wrinkle rings without torsion.
